observation: A study on faithfulness of document-grounded podcast generation found even GPT-4o achieved only 3.89/5.0 on a faithfulness scale, worst in academic-domain source material (3.38/5.0); a catch-and-repair turn-level grounding classifier recovered ~5-13% relative faithfulness without hurting coverage.
claim: Riemann should never trust a single LLM pass to stay grounded in the source for any generated content, especially the technical/academic material Sam's coursework involves; a cheap span-citation check is directly reusable since the tree already carries source_span provenance.
mechanism: Even top models frequently generate ungrounded content under elaboration; a turn/sentence-level check against source spans catches and can repair drift.
population: general (document-to-podcast generation benchmark, multiple domains including academic)
context: single arXiv paper, not yet peer-reviewed, concrete methodology and numbers

implications.text: Implement a cheap sentence/claim-level check that generated text traces to a source_span already present in the tree, for any generated summary or future audio content.

observation: Multiple 2024-2026 papers converge on LLM length-control being unreliable: GPT-4-class models violate explicit word-count constraints roughly half the time in some benchmarks, and changing a target from 600 to 610 words can flip pass/fail for a substantial number of test cases.
claim: Riemann's L1 'target word band' contract cannot be trusted to the prompt alone; build.py's existing validate-and-retry pattern must be extended to a deterministic word-count check with a targeted retry, not just JSON schema validation.
mechanism: Sub-word tokenization means models don't reliably 'count' words, and training data underrepresents strict length-constrained examples, making prompt-only length compliance brittle.

implications.text: After generating L0/L1 text, check word_count against the target band programmatically; if outside the band, do one targeted retry stating the exact delta to fix.

observation: Chain-of-Density (Adams et al. 2023) has GPT-4 iteratively rewrite a summary to fold in 1-3 missing salient entities per step without increasing length; a human preference study (100 CNN/DailyMail articles) found people prefer denser CoD summaries over vanilla-prompt summaries, approaching human-reference density, with less lead bias.
claim: A 2-3 step density pass (draft, identify missing salient entities, rewrite at the same length) should replace a single-shot prompt for L0/L1 generation, controlling information density independent of length.
mechanism: Iterative densification without length growth forces compression/fusion of existing content to make room for missing salient information, rather than simply adding more words.
context: single well-known paper, methodologically concrete, 500 human-annotated summaries

implications.text: Use a Chain-of-Density-style 2-3 pass generation for L0/L1 instead of a single-shot summarize prompt, composing with the length-retry loop.

observation: Automatically-generated concept maps show 50-80% concept-relevance versus 65-90% for semi-automated extraction; in a clinical-reasoning study of 40 student-made concept maps, diagnostic accuracy correlated with connection quality (relational-validity rubric), not with the number of concepts or connections, and 82% of students defaulted to bare node lists with no connections unless pushed.
claim: If Riemann's tree is ever rendered as a node-link diagram, the tree's own parent/child edges are structurally guaranteed and safe, but any additional cross-links an LLM proposes between non-adjacent nodes need the same relational-correctness skepticism as a from-scratch concept map — edges, not nodes, are the risk.
mechanism: Connection quality, not node/edge count, is what predicts whether a concept map is actually correct; auto-generated edges specifically show low precision/recall against a gold standard in at least one clinical-domain study.
population: general (clinical-reasoning education, medical students); general concept-map generation benchmarks
context: mixed: one study read in full, clinical precision/recall figures from a blocked abstract

implications.text: Treat any LLM-proposed cross-link (beyond the tree's own parent/child edges) as an unverified concept-map edge requiring schema validation and a repair pass, weighting edge correctness over node count.

observation: ISO 24495-1:2023 is a real, citable international plain-language standard defining four pillars — findable, understandable, usable, relevant — distinct from targeting a single readability formula like Flesch-Kincaid.
claim: L0/L1 generation prompts should adopt ISO 24495-1's four pillars as an explicit checklist, not just a target reading-grade number.
mechanism: A multi-pillar plain-language standard captures structural/navigational and relevance properties that a pure readability-score target misses.

implications.text: Add findable/understandable/usable/relevant as an explicit prompt checklist for L0/L1 generation, alongside any word-count/density targets.

observation: LLM-as-judge is the dominant cheap-evaluation paradigm for summary faithfulness/coherence, but has documented reliability problems (self-preference, length bias, self-inconsistency); in the podcast-faithfulness study, the LLM judge correlated with human ratings at only 0.63 Pearson.
claim: LLM-as-judge should never silently gate what gets shown to the user (e.g. auto-hiding a summary judged 'unfaithful') without a deterministic backstop; prefer deterministic checks (word count, span-citation presence, schema validity) wherever one exists.
mechanism: LLM judges are moderately but not highly correlated with human judgment and carry known systematic biases, so they are usable as a monitoring signal but not as ground truth.

implications.text: Prefer deterministic checks (length, span-citation, schema) over LLM-judge checks; reserve LLM-as-judge for softer qualities like tone/coherence where no deterministic proxy exists.

observation: A study of LLM-generated simplification/ELI5-style text found it tends to flatten polysemous (multi-sense) words into a single implied meaning, silently dropping the signal that a term has more than one valid sense in context — a more dangerous failure than an obviously-wrong answer because users assume LLM output is both correct and complete.
claim: Any future 'explain like I'm X' or personalized-analogy feature must flag terms appearing in multiple L3 chunks with materially different senses, rather than silently simplifying past genuine polysemy.
mechanism: Simplification collapses multi-valid answers into a false single answer, and this failure is specifically dangerous because it is silent and plausible-looking, not obviously wrong.
context: single arXiv paper with a clear, testable claim

implications.text: Flag terms appearing in more than one L3 chunk with materially different senses during generation, and don't silently simplify past that ambiguity — directly relevant to overloaded engineering terminology.
